paragraphs: Topological data analysis describes the shape of data across different scales. Persistent homology tracks how that shape changes as a parameter varies. For some datasets, however, several parameters matter together, such as feature scale and density. The paper addresses how to turn this richer description into vectors that standard machine learning methods can use.

Existing representations can discard much of the information by reducing the problem to one parameter, or rely on heuristics that may react unpredictably to noise. The proposed framework uses mathematical decompositions of multiparameter persistent homology to construct informative representations. It includes previous approaches within a broader framework and provides efficient algorithms for computing the resulting descriptors.

The authors establish theoretical stability guarantees, connecting the representations to a principled treatment of perturbations. Numerical experiments on several real datasets examine statistical convergence, prediction accuracy, and running time. Together, these contributions make the framework useful for bringing multiscale geometric information into machine learning while addressing both computational cost and sensitivity to noise.
neurips-2023-a-framework-for-fast-and-st.tldr: A general framework turns multiparameter topological descriptions into efficiently computed machine learning representations with theoretical stability guarantees.

paragraphs: Federated learning can lose useful participants when their devices lack enough memory to train the shared model. Excluding those devices also excludes their data and computation, potentially reducing accuracy and introducing bias or unfairness. Training only selected model parameters reduces memory requirements, but it can restrict how different parameters learn to work together.

The paper argues that this restriction makes existing subset-training techniques inefficient. In the authors' evaluation, training a smaller model that every device can update end to end is better than applying those techniques. Their proposed method instead successively freezes and trains model parameters, reducing the resources needed at each device while preserving enough interaction between the parameters being learned.

Extensive experiments report an accuracy improvement of 52.4 percentage points over the state of the art. This is an experimental result, rather than a guarantee for every device population. Its significance is that accommodating constrained devices need not simply mean shrinking the shared model: changing the training schedule can help combine the capacity available across participating devices.
neurips-2023-aggregating-capacity-in-fl-.tldr: Successively freezing and training model parameters helps memory-constrained federated devices participate while substantially improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Look-alike clustering replaces an individual's sensitive features with average values from a cluster of similar individuals. The paper studies what this transformation does to a model's ability to generalize. The central question is whether learning from these anonymous representations necessarily sacrifices predictive quality, or whether averaging can sometimes help the learned model.

The authors derive a precise analysis in a high-dimensional asymptotic setting: the number of training examples grows in proportion to the number of features. They use the Convex Gaussian Minimax Theorem to characterize generalization error and understand how different model components contribute to it. This provides a theoretical account of the consequences of replacing individual features with cluster averages.

In certain high-dimensional regimes, the analysis shows that this replacement acts as regularization and improves generalization. The benefit is conditional on the regime studied, rather than a universal property of anonymization. Finite-sample numerical experiments closely match the asymptotic predictions with only a few hundred examples, supporting the theory's relevance beyond an infinite-data limit.
neurips-2023-anonymous-learning-via-look.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis shows that replacing sensitive features with cluster averages can improve generalization by acting as regularization in certain regimes.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent changes ordinary training by clipping each example's gradient and adding noise. These changes protect privacy but can reduce predictive performance. One approach to improving the tradeoff is to give the model useful prior knowledge before it learns from private data, often by learning that knowledge from public real-world images.

This paper investigates a different source of prior knowledge: images produced by random processes. Its proposed method, DP-RandP, uses a three-phase approach to learn priors from those generated images and transfer them to private data. The central idea is that useful preparation for image classification can come from generated visual structure, rather than requiring real-world public training images.

The authors report new state-of-the-art accuracy for training from scratch on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, MedMNIST, and ImageNet across privacy budgets from one to eight. At a privacy budget of one on CIFAR10, accuracy rises from the previous best reported 60.6% to 72.3%. These findings support random-process priors as a practical way to improve accuracy under the evaluated privacy constraints.
neurips-2023-differentially-private-imag.tldr: DP-RandP transfers priors learned from randomly generated images to improve differentially private image classification.

paragraphs: Some concepts are difficult to convey to a language model with ordinary words alone. X-Prompt proposes expanding the prompting vocabulary with learned imaginary words that can represent such concepts. These words appear alongside natural language instructions, giving users additional ways to specify what they want the model to express.

The important design goal is reuse across different prompts. A learned word should remain useful when placed in a context that was not seen during its training. The authors introduce context-augmented learning to develop this general usability. They distinguish this objective from soft prompts intended to fit an existing data distribution: the imaginary words are designed to function across unfamiliar prompt contexts.

The paper tests the approach through zero-shot language style customization. Its reported results are promising and suggest that an extensible vocabulary could support more expressive interaction with language models. The evidence is presented as a case study demonstrating potential, rather than as a guarantee that any hard-to-describe concept can be reliably captured or reused in every setting.
neurips-2023-extensible-prompts-for-lang.tldr: X-Prompt learns reusable imaginary words to express concepts beyond ordinary language, with promising results for zero-shot style customization.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares probability distributions while also describing how to move mass from one to the other. This paper introduces min-SWGG, a proxy for the squared Wasserstein distance built from a transport map induced by a selected one-dimensional projection. The approach aims to make the comparison inexpensive while retaining an associated transport plan.

The authors connect the construction to generalized Wasserstein geodesics whose pivot distribution lies on a line. They derive an exact closed-form Wasserstein distance for the special case where one input distribution is supported on a line. This result enables a fast computational procedure that can be optimized with gradient descent.

The paper establishes an upper-bound relationship to Wasserstein distance and reports computational complexity similar to Sliced-Wasserstein, with the added output of a transport plan. It also investigates metric, convergence, computational, and topological properties. Experiments involving gradient flows, shape matching, and image colorization support the method's usefulness in settings where both distribution comparison and an explicit correspondence between distributions matter.
neurips-2023-fast-optimal-transport-thro.tldr: Min-SWGG uses one-dimensional projections to provide a fast Wasserstein-distance proxy together with an associated transport plan.

paragraphs: Contrastive methods learn graph-node representations by comparing augmented views of the graph. The paper identifies a restriction in common augmentations: they behave like low-pass filters, emphasizing only part of the graph's eigen-spectrum. Tasks that depend on other spectral components can therefore receive less useful representations, even when the overall learning approach performs well elsewhere.

FiGURe introduces filter-based augmentations that capture different spectral components. The authors show that the same model weights can be shared across these augmentations, reducing computation. They also address the expense of high-dimensional node representations by using random Fourier feature projections, recovering good performance with lower-dimensional embeddings.

Across the datasets considered, FiGURe reports an average gain of up to 4.4% over state-of-the-art unsupervised models. The evaluation includes both homophilic and heterophilic graphs, covering different relationships between connected nodes. The findings support broadening the information exposed through augmentation while controlling the cost of processing multiple views and storing large representations.
neurips-2023-figure-simple-and-efficient.tldr: FiGURe improves unsupervised graph representations with diverse spectral filters, shared weights, and efficient lower-dimensional embeddings.

paragraphs: Geometric learning problems involve different kinds of objects, including points, directions, translations, and rotations. A useful architecture needs to handle these objects while respecting the symmetries of three-dimensional space. The Geometric Algebra Transformer, or GATr, addresses this need with a shared mathematical representation for geometric data and the operations acting on it.

GATr represents inputs, outputs, and intermediate states using projective geometric algebra, also called Clifford algebra. This supplies a 16-dimensional vector space for common geometric objects and operators. The architecture is equivariant under the Euclidean symmetry group E(3), meaning its outputs transform consistently with the corresponding transformations of its inputs.

The authors combine this geometric structure with a Transformer architecture intended to remain versatile and scalable. They demonstrate it on n-body modeling, wall-shear-stress estimation over large arterial meshes, and robotic motion planning. Across the reported problems, GATr consistently outperforms both non-geometric and equivariant baselines in error, data efficiency, and scalability, supporting the usefulness of one architecture across varied geometric tasks.
neurips-2023-geometric-algebra-transform.tldr: GATr combines geometric algebra with Transformers to handle varied three-dimensional objects while respecting Euclidean symmetries.

paragraphs: GINO learns a solution operator for large-scale partial differential equations whose geometries vary. It represents each input shape through a signed distance function and combines graph-based and Fourier-based neural operators. This arrangement connects the irregular grids associated with complex shapes to regular latent grids where Fourier operations can be applied efficiently.

The graph operator moves information into and out of that regular representation. An optimized hashing implementation supports learning in a shared compressed space, reducing computation and memory costs. The architecture is discretization-invariant, allowing a trained model to operate across discretizations and resolutions of the continuous domain.

The authors evaluate GINO on three-dimensional vehicle aerodynamics with Reynolds numbers reaching five million, training surface-pressure prediction with 500 data points. Cost-accuracy experiments report a 26,000-fold speedup over optimized GPU-based CFD simulators for computing drag coefficients. On new combinations of shapes and inlet velocities, GINO reduces error by one fourth compared with deep neural network approaches. These results demonstrate the method's potential for accelerating the evaluated fluid-simulation tasks.
neurips-2023-geometry-informed-neural-op.tldr: GINO combines graph and Fourier neural operators to learn efficient PDE solutions across varying three-dimensional geometries and discretizations.

paragraphs: Noise added during optimization need not be independent from one training step to the next. Some practical methods for differential privacy, including DP-FTRL, use matrix factorizations that create linear correlations across iterations. These methods are particularly relevant when privacy amplification techniques are infeasible, as can occur in federated learning.

The paper develops a simplified setting that isolates the effect of this correlated noise on gradient descent. It analyzes both convex and non-convex objectives, providing tighter results than prior analyses. The analysis also recovers several important special cases exactly, including gradient descent with anticorrelated perturbations.

The authors then use these results to design new matrix factorizations for differentially private optimization and demonstrate their benefits theoretically and empirically. The contribution connects an explanation of noisy optimization dynamics to a concrete design choice in privacy-preserving training. Understanding how noise is related across steps can therefore help improve the optimization mechanisms that inject it, rather than treating noise solely through its magnitude.
neurips-2023-gradient-descent-with-linea.tldr: A tighter analysis of gradient descent with correlated noise guides new matrix factorizations for differentially private optimization.

paragraphs: Image classifiers discard information when converting an image into a label. This paper investigates the hypothesis that successful classification often depends on first focusing on the most informative region. Studying six networks ranging from AlexNet to CLIP, the authors find that appropriate image framing can enable correct classification of 98.91% of ImageNet images.

The study also reveals positional biases in datasets, including a strong center bias in ImageNet-A and ObjectNet. These findings motivate a test-time augmentation method that explicitly makes models zoom into images before predicting. In the reported comparison, this method is more interpretable, more accurate, and faster than MEMO.

The authors additionally introduce ImageNet-Hard, a benchmark built around images that remain challenging even when optimal zooming is allowed. It challenges state-of-the-art classifiers, including large vision-language models. The benchmark separates the substantial opportunity offered by better framing from the difficulty that remains after exploiting it, providing a way to evaluate recognition failures that cannot simply be resolved through optimal zooming.
neurips-2023-imagenet-hard-the-hardest-i.tldr: A study of image framing motivates a zoom-based prediction method and ImageNet-Hard, a benchmark that remains difficult even with optimal zooming.

paragraphs: CLIP learns transferable visual representations from paired images and text. Its training commonly varies the images through augmentation while keeping their descriptions fixed. This means a given image repeatedly appears with the same wording, limiting the diversity of language the model encounters for the concepts shown in that image.

Language augmented CLIP, or LaCLIP, adds variation on the text side. The authors use a large language model's in-context learning ability to rewrite image descriptions with different vocabulary and sentence structures while preserving their key meanings. Training randomly selects either the original description or a rewritten version for each image.

Experiments on CC3M, CC12M, RedCaps, and LAION-400M show improved transfer performance without additional computation or memory overhead during training. For ImageNet zero-shot accuracy, the abstract reports improvements over CLIP of 8.2% with CC12M and 2.4% with LAION-400M. The findings support language diversity as a useful training ingredient: several ways of describing the same image can improve the representations learned from image-text pairs.
neurips-2023-improving-clip-training-wit.tldr: LaCLIP improves CLIP transfer performance by randomly training on original image captions or meaning-preserving language-model rewrites.

paragraphs: A common approach to zero-shot segmentation first proposes image regions and then asks CLIP to classify them. The paper finds that CLIP often gives similar predictions to different masks from the same image. Because its training supervision describes whole images, it can overlook the distinctions between proposed regions, producing many false positives.

Mask-aware Fine-tuning, or MAFT, addresses this mismatch. Its Image-Proposals CLIP Encoder processes an image together with arbitrary numbers of mask proposals. A mask-aware loss encourages sensitivity to the proposals, while a self-distillation loss helps preserve transferability. The method adds no new parameters during fine-tuning and can be incorporated into most existing approaches.

On unseen classes, the authors report mIoU scores of 50.4% on COCO, 81.8% on Pascal-VOC, and 8.7% on ADE20K, with respective reported gains of 8.2, 3.2, and 4.3 percentage points. These results show that adapting CLIP to region-level distinctions can substantially improve segmentation while retaining its ability to transfer to unseen classes.
neurips-2023-learning-mask-aware-clip-re.tldr: MAFT fine-tunes CLIP to distinguish proposed image regions while preserving transferability, improving zero-shot segmentation in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bandit learners make decisions with feedback limited to the actions they take. This paper studies how a learner can improve across multiple adversarial tasks when those tasks share useful structure. An outer learning process adjusts the starting point and other hyperparameters of an inner learner that handles decisions within each task.

For multi-armed bandits, the method tunes a Tsallis-entropy generalization of Exp3. Its task-averaged regret improves when the best actions identified in hindsight have low entropy, capturing one form of similarity across tasks. For bandit linear optimization, the method tunes online mirror descent with self-concordant barrier regularizers, with guarantees tied to a measure determined by the action space.

The theoretical contribution shows that follow-the-leader, combined with two levels of low-dimensional hyperparameter tuning, can learn the quantities needed to control the inner learner's regret. This remains possible despite non-Lipschitz and sometimes non-convex Bregman divergences in the analysis. The resulting guarantees make the benefits of cross-task adaptation conditional on explicit measures of shared structure.
neurips-2023-meta-learning-adversarial-b.tldr: Meta-learning tunes adversarial bandit algorithms across tasks, with regret improvements linked to explicit measures of task similarity.

paragraphs: Exploration becomes difficult when an agent receives high-dimensional observations and useful external rewards are rare. Intrinsic rewards encourage exploration by estimating how novel a state, transition, or trajectory is. This paper connects such novelty estimates to conditional prediction: predicting missing information from whatever parts of an observation or sequence remain visible.

The authors use the perspective that masked prediction objectives can estimate pseudo-likelihood, a probability-related quantity built from conditional predictions. They show that existing intrinsic reward approaches can be understood as special cases using different masking distributions. Their framework, Masked Input Modeling for Exploration, or MIMEx, makes that distribution a flexible design choice.

Changing which information is hidden controls the difficulty of the underlying prediction task and therefore how novelty is estimated. On a suite of challenging sparse-reward visuomotor tasks, MIMEx can outperform competitive baselines. The contribution is both a common explanation for existing exploration rewards and a way to derive new ones by adjusting the conditional prediction problem.
neurips-2023-mimex-intrinsic-rewards-fro.tldr: MIMEx derives exploration rewards from masked prediction tasks whose difficulty can be adjusted through the masking distribution.

paragraphs: Teaching a robot team from demonstrations is difficult when each robot observes only part of the environment. Communication can improve coordination, but existing multi-agent demonstration frameworks may require experts to demonstrate both task actions and communication actions. This adds the burden of specifying how robots should communicate within a known message space.

MixTURE learns collaborative behavior from human expert data while also learning communication among the robots. Its key component is an automatically learned communication policy supported by a reverse model that maximizes mutual information. This model helps account for the expert demonstrations without requiring human-generated communication data or an auxiliary reward function.

The authors report that MixTURE outperforms relevant baselines across diverse human-generated data in complex heterogeneous domains. They also report approximately 44% lower human workload and a 46% higher usability score. These findings support the practical value of learning communication alongside task behavior: experts can demonstrate how to accomplish a collaborative task while the framework takes on more of the work of developing coordination.
neurips-2023-mixed-initiative-multiagent.tldr: MixTURE learns robot-team behavior and communication from human task demonstrations, reducing expert workload in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Multi-hop knowledge graph question answering finds answer nodes by following several relationships from an initial node. Existing graph neural network methods often pass information along the path already explored. The paper argues that this past-oriented view misses useful surrounding context, especially when node names are ambiguous, pronoun-like, or encrypted.

NuTrea introduces a tree-search-based graph neural network that probes subtree regions it has not yet reached. Information from these regions enriches the representations built from previous steps, helping the model consider broader context when selecting paths. It also introduces Relation Frequency-Inverse Entity Frequency embeddings, which use global relationship information to better characterize otherwise uninformative nodes.

Experiments on three major multi-hop question-answering benchmarks demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, while additional analyses support its expressiveness and robustness. The two components address complementary sources of uncertainty: what lies beyond the current search path, and what an ambiguous node represents within the larger graph. Together, they support answering complex natural-language questions through more context-informed graph search.
neurips-2023-nutrea-neural-tree-search-f.tldr: NuTrea improves multi-hop knowledge graph question answering by probing unexplored subtrees and representing ambiguous nodes through global relationship context.

paragraphs: Ranking distillation transfers knowledge from teacher ranking models to other models. Unlike ordinary classification, this can use information about the ordering of items. Although many methods have been proposed, inconsistent tasks, datasets, and evaluation practices make it difficult to determine which advances hold up under comparable conditions.

RD-Suite provides a systematic benchmark for this problem. The authors first examine representative prior methods and raise three questions about methodology and reproducibility. Their benchmark then brings together four large real-world datasets, covering textual and numeric inputs as well as standard distillation and distillation transfer.

The suite includes benchmark results, datasets with teacher scores, and evaluation scripts. Its findings challenge some common assumptions in ranking distillation, making the evaluation framework itself a contribution to understanding the field. Providing shared teacher outputs and evaluation procedures gives future studies a more consistent basis for comparison, helping distinguish methodological improvements from differences in how experiments are set up.
neurips-2023-rd-suite-a-benchmark-for-ra.tldr: RD-Suite standardizes ranking-distillation evaluation across four real-world datasets, with teacher scores, evaluation scripts, and results that challenge existing assumptions.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning is useful when labels are available for groups of examples but detailed labels for individual examples are limited. In video analysis, this can mean learning useful frame representations without extensive frame-level annotation. The paper argues that existing methods emphasize relationships and aggregation while overlooking information inherent in the multiple-instance learning problem.

RGMIL introduces Regressor-Guided Pooling, an aggregation method that uses information from the regressor to describe that problem more accurately. The pooling mechanism adds no new parameters and is designed to reflect how humans reason through similar inference problems. It aims to improve both group-level decisions and the representations needed for individual predictions.

The authors report strong results on more than 20 benchmarks, with average bag-level accuracy close to one, plus extensive MMNIST experiments. They also demonstrate long-sequence instance predictions and performance comparable to leading supervised models in complex applications. The results support the possibility of competitive instance-level learning when the model structure accurately represents the multiple-instance problem.
neurips-2023-rgmil-guide-your-multiple-i.tldr: RGMIL uses regressor-guided pooling to improve multiple-instance learning, achieving strong group-level and instance-level results with limited annotation.

paragraphs: Class-incremental semantic segmentation learns new pixel categories over successive training stages. The paper highlights a sampling problem: each stage includes images containing its current foreground classes and excludes images without them. This overrepresents those classes and biases predictions toward them, adding another difficulty alongside forgetting and changes in the meaning of background.

STAR stores a compact prototype and necessary statistics for each past class. It replays these prototypes and repeats background pixels at suitable frequencies to bring the current training distribution closer to that of the complete dataset. This addresses the imbalance without relying on storage of raw images from earlier stages.

Two additional losses help preserve old-class features while allowing new learning and increase separation between similar old and new classes. Compared with previous raw-image replay methods, STAR uses over 100 times less storage while improving performance. Experiments on Pascal VOC 2012 and ADE20K surpass previous state-of-the-art methods, supporting distribution reconstruction as an important part of incremental segmentation.
neurips-2023-saving-100x-storage-prototy.tldr: STAR corrects incremental segmentation's class-distribution bias through compact prototype replay, improving performance while using over 100 times less storage than raw-image replay.

paragraphs: Regularized training often corresponds to choosing the most probable model parameters under a posterior distribution. Yet predictions depend on the function those parameters define. The paper examines this distinction: the most probable parameter setting need not produce the most probable function, so optimizing one can differ from optimizing the other.

The authors show that parameter-posterior maximization depends strongly on how a model is parameterized. A reparameterization can make any chosen parameter setting maximize that posterior. They therefore investigate directly estimating the most likely function implied by the model and data, while examining both the benefits and drawbacks of this alternative.

Direct function-space estimation can produce pathological solutions with neural networks. The paper proves conditions under which it behaves well and develops a scalable approximation. Under those conditions, the authors find that function-space MAP estimation can yield flatter minima, better generalization, and greater robustness to overfitting. The contribution is a conditional route toward prediction-focused estimation, together with an explanation of why that route requires care.
neurips-2023-should-we-learn-most-likely.tldr: Function-space MAP estimation can improve generalization under established conditions, but applying it directly to neural networks can also produce pathological solutions.

paragraphs: A bandit policy can perform well on average yet still have a meaningful chance of accumulating unusually large regret. This paper studies the relationship between average performance and that tail risk. It considers worst-case optimality, instance-dependent consistency, and how quickly the probability of large regret decreases as the decision horizon grows.

The authors characterize how the order of expected regret determines achievable tail-probability decay in both worst-case and instance-dependent settings. They propose a policy with adjustable expected-regret rates that achieves optimal tail risk for any regret threshold. For the specified parameter ranges, large-regret probabilities decay exponentially in a polynomial of the horizon, at a rate proved best achievable.

The analysis also extends to rewards containing an arm-specific mean, independent noise, and a time-varying baseline. Its central implication is a tradeoff: accepting more suboptimality or weaker instance-dependent consistency can create room for lighter tails. This gives a theoretical basis for selecting policies according to both expected performance and exposure to unusually poor outcomes.
neurips-2023-stochastic-multi-armed-band.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal tradeoffs between expected bandit regret and large-regret risk, and constructs a policy attaining the best achievable tail decay.

paragraphs: Selective classification lets a model decline difficult inputs so that the predictions it does make are more reliable. Coverage describes how much of the input population it accepts, while selective risk measures errors among accepted predictions. Ensembles work well in this setting, but their practical success has lacked a solid explanation.

The paper starts from an empirical observation: much of the ensemble's improvement comes from highly ambiguous samples on which its members disagree. Motivated by this pattern, the authors prove that an ensemble has lower selective risk than a member model for every coverage level within a particular range, provided their assumptions hold.

The result is conditional and applies over the stated coverage range. Establishing it is technically difficult because selective risk is a non-convex function of model predictions. Systematic experiments in computer vision and natural language processing support both the assumptions and theoretical findings. The work links ensemble reliability to the behavior of its members on the most ambiguous inputs.
neurips-2023-top-ambiguity-samples-matte.tldr: Under stated assumptions, ensembles reduce selective-classification risk across a coverage range, with highly ambiguous inputs helping explain their advantage.

paragraphs: Training a ReLU network can involve changing activation patterns, plateaus, and other nonlinear behavior. These dynamics are difficult to analyze because both the model and its optimization landscape are complex. Much previous theory therefore examines only a local part of training or replaces the network with an approximately linear model.

This paper characterizes the full training trajectory in a specific setting: a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient flow on linearly separable data. Its analysis begins at random initialization and continues through convergence. Even with this relatively simple network and dataset structure, the authors identify four distinct phases of learning.

The phases reveal an overall progression in which learning first simplifies and then becomes more complex. The theory captures initial condensation, movement from saddles to plateaus, escape from plateaus, and changes in activation patterns. These results show how several nonlinear phenomena can arise within one complete account of training. Their scope remains the stated two-layer, gradient-flow, linearly separable setting.
neurips-2023-understanding-multi-phase-o.tldr: A full analysis of two-layer ReLU training under gradient flow reveals four phases and captures nonlinear behavior from initialization to convergence.

paragraphs: Encoder-decoder Transformers face input-length constraints because attention ordinarily considers every input token. Unlimiformer wraps a pretrained model and moves cross-attention retrieval into a single nearest-neighbor index. Each attention head in every decoder layer retrieves its top matching keys, with the returned scores corresponding to the attention dot products.

The index can reside in CPU or GPU memory and supports queries in sublinear time. This makes practically unlimited input sequences indexable without requiring each attention head to inspect every key. The approach extends pretrained models without adding learned weights or modifying their code, providing a way to expand usable context around an existing model.

The authors evaluate Unlimiformer on long-document and book-summarization benchmarks. They demonstrate processing BookSum inputs containing 500,000 tokens without truncation at test time and report improvements to models such as BART and Longformer. The results establish that retrieval-based cross-attention can make very long inputs usable in these tasks, with the concrete demonstration grounding the broader claim of practically unlimited input length.
neurips-2023-unlimiformer-long-range-tra.tldr: Unlimiformer replaces exhaustive cross-attention with nearest-neighbor retrieval, enabling pretrained models to process inputs demonstrated at 500,000 tokens without truncation.
